nodes.name: $k$-colouring
nodes.statement: A {\em $k$-colouring} of a graph~$G=(V,E)$ is a mapping $c:V\to \{1,\dots,k\}$ such that $c(u)\neq c(v)$ whenever $uv\in E$.

nodes.name: hereditary graph class
nodes.statement: A class is hereditary if it closed under vertex deletion.

nodes.name: ${\cal H}$-free graph
nodes.statement: Graphs with no induced subgraph isomorphic to a graph in a set~${\cal H}$ are said to be {\em ${\cal H}$-free}.
differentia: no induced subgraph isomorphic to a graph in a set~${\cal H}$

nodes.name: bigenic graph class
nodes.statement: Kr\'al' et al.~\cite{KKTW01} also initiated a complexity study of {\sc Colouring} for graph classes defined by two forbidden induced subgraphs~$H_1$ and~$H_2$. Such graph classes are said to be {\em bigenic}.
nodes.statement_short: A graph class is bigenic when it is defined by exactly two forbidden induced subgraphs.
differentia: defined by two forbidden induced subgraphs~$H_1$ and~$H_2$

nodes.name: almost classified graph
nodes.statement: We say that a connected graph~$H_1$ is {\em almost classified} if {\sc Colouring} on $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs is known to be either polynomial-time solvable or \NP-complete for all but finitely many connected graphs~$H_2$.
nodes.statement_short: $H_1$ is almost classified when only finitely many connected $H_2$ leave the complexity of Colouring on $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs unknown.
differentia: {\sc Colouring} on $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs is known to be either polynomial-time solvable or \NP-complete for all but finitely many connected graphs~$H_2$

nodes.name: complement of a graph
nodes.statement: The {\em complement}~$\overline{G}$ of~$G$ is the graph with vertex set~$V(G)$ and an edge between two distinct vertices if and only if these two vertices are not adjacent in~$G$.
differentia: an edge between two distinct vertices if and only if these two vertices are not adjacent in~$G$

nodes.name: induced subgraph $G[S]$
nodes.statement: For a subset $S\subseteq V$, we let~$G[S]$ denote the subgraph of~$G$ {\em induced} by~$S$, which has vertex set~$S$ and edge set $\{uv\; |\; u,v\in S, uv\in E\}$.
differentia: edge set $\{uv\; |\; u,v\in S, uv\in E\}$

nodes.name: $(H_1,\ldots,H_p)$-free graph
nodes.statement: Let $\{H_1,\ldots,H_p\}$ be a set of graphs. A graph~$G$ is {\em $(H_1,\ldots,H_p)$-free} if~$G$ has no induced subgraph isomorphic to a graph in $\{H_1,\ldots,H_p\}$. If~$p=1$, we may write $H_1$-free instead of $(H_1)$-free.
differentia: $G$ has no induced subgraph isomorphic to a graph in $\{H_1,\ldots,H_p\}$

nodes.name: disjoint union
nodes.statement: The {\em disjoint union} $G+\nobreak H$ of two vertex-disjoint graphs~$G$ and~$H$ is the graph $(V(G)\cup V(H), E(G)\cup E(H))$. The disjoint union of~$r$ copies of a graph~$G$ is denoted by~$rG$.

nodes.name: linear forest
nodes.statement: A {\em linear forest} is the disjoint union of one or more paths.

nodes.name: $C_r$, $K_r$, $P_r$, $K_{r,s}$, triangle, claw
nodes.statement: The graphs~$C_r$, $K_r$ and~$P_r$ denote the cycle, complete graph and path on~$r$ vertices, respectively. The graph~$K_3$ is also known as the {\em triangle}. The graph~$K_{r,s}$ denotes the complete bipartite graph with partition classes of size~$r$ and~$s$, respectively. The graph~$K_{1,3}$ is also called the {\em claw}.
nodes.statement_short: Notation for cycles $C_r$, cliques $K_r$, paths $P_r$ and complete bipartite graphs $K_{r,s}$, with $K_3$ the triangle and $K_{1,3}$ the claw.

nodes.name: subdivided claw $S_{h,i,j}$
nodes.statement: The graph~$S_{h,i,j}$, for $1\leq h\leq i\leq j$, denotes the {\em subdivided claw}, that is, the tree that has only one vertex~$x$ of degree~$3$ and exactly three leaves, which are of distance~$h$,~$i$ and~$j$ from~$x$, respectively. Observe that $S_{1,1,1}=K_{1,3}$. The graph~$S_{1,1,2}$ is also known as the {\em fork} or the {\em chair}.
nodes.statement_short: $S_{h,i,j}$ is the tree obtained from a claw by subdividing its three legs to lengths $h,i,j$.
differentia: has only one vertex~$x$ of degree~$3$
exactly three leaves, which are of distance~$h$,~$i$ and~$j$ from~$x$, respectively

nodes.name: $T_{h,i,j}$ (paw, bull, net, hammer)
nodes.statement:
The graph~$T_{h,i,j}$ with $0\leq h\leq i\leq j$ denotes the graph with vertices $a_0,\ldots,a_h$, $b_0,\ldots,b_i$ and $c_0,\ldots,c_j$ and edges $a_0b_0$, $b_0c_0$, $c_0a_0$, $a_pa_{p+1}$ for $p \in \{0,\ldots, h-
obreak1\}$, $b_pb_{p+1}$ for $p\in\{0,\ldots,i-
obreak 1\}$ and $c_pc_{p+1}$ for $p\in\{0,\ldots,j-
obreak 1\}$. Note that $T_{0,0,0}=C_3$. The graph $T_{0,0,1}=\overline{P_1+P_3}$ is known as the {\em paw}, the graph~$T_{0,1,1}$ as the {\em bull}, the graph~$T_{1,1,1}$ as the {\em net}, and the graph~$T_{0,0,2}$ is known as the {\em hammer}; see also  igurename~ef{fig:Thij-examples}.
nodes.statement_short: $T_{h,i,j}$ is a triangle with three pendant paths of lengths $h,i,j$; small cases are the triangle, paw, bull, net and hammer.
differentia:
edges $a_0b_0$, $b_0c_0$, $c_0a_0$, $a_pa_{p+1}$ for $p \in \{0,\ldots, h-
obreak1\}$, $b_pb_{p+1}$ for $p\in\{0,\ldots,i-
obreak 1\}$ and $c_pc_{p+1}$ for $p\in\{0,\ldots,j-
obreak 1\}$

nodes.name: the class ${\cal T}$
nodes.statement: Let~${\cal T}$ be the class of graphs every component of which is isomorphic to a graph~$T_{h,i,j}$ for some $1\leq h\leq i\leq j$ or a path~$P_r$ for some $r\geq 1$.
differentia: every component of which is isomorphic to a graph~$T_{h,i,j}$ for some $1\leq h\leq i\leq j$ or a path~$P_r$ for some $r\geq 1$

nodes.name: complete split graph
nodes.statement: As observed in~\cite{GP14}, a minor modification of this construction yields that {\sc List Colouring} is \NP-complete for complete split graphs, which are the graphs obtained from complete bipartite graphs by changing one of the bipartition classes into a clique.
nodes.statement_short: A complete split graph is a complete bipartite graph with one side turned into a clique.
nodes.genus: graphs obtained from complete bipartite graphs
differentia: changing one of the bipartition classes into a clique

nodes.name: Colouring
nodes.statement: The {\sc Colouring} problem that of deciding whether a given graph~$G$ has a $k$-colouring for a given integer~$k$. If~$k$ is fixed, then we write $k$-{\sc Colouring} instead.
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a given graph admits a $k$-colouring for a given $k$; with $k$ fixed the problem is $k$-Colouring.

nodes.name: Precolouring Extension
nodes.statement: For the first problem, we are given a graph~$G$, an integer~$k$ and a $k$-colouring~$c'$ defined on an induced subgraph of~$G$. The question is whether~$G$ has a $k$-colouring~$c$ extending~$c'$.
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a partial $k$-colouring of an induced subgraph extends to the whole graph.
nodes.origin_citation: classical decision problem; see Golovach, Johnson, Paulusma & Song 2017

nodes.name: List Colouring
nodes.statement: For the second problem, each vertex~$u$ of the input graph~$G$ has a list~$L(u)$ of colours. Here the question is whether~$G$ has a colouring~$c$ that respects~$L$, that is, with $c(u)\in L(u)$ for all $u\in V(G)$.
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether a graph has a proper colouring choosing each vertex's colour from its own list.

nodes.name: Not-All-Equal $3$-Satisfiability with positive literals only
nodes.statement: We first describe the construction of~\cite{GH09}, which uses a reduction from the \NP-complete~\cite{Sc78} problem {\sc Not-All-Equal $3$-Satisfiability} with positive literals only. To define this problem, let $X= \{x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n\}$ be a set of logical variables, and let ${\cal C} = \{C_1, C_2,\ldots, C_m\}$ be a set of $3$-literal clauses over~$X$ in which all literals are positive and every literal appears at most once in each clause. The question is whether~$X$ has a truth assignment such that each clause in~${\cal C}$ contains at least one true literal and at least one false literal. If so, we say that such a truth assignment is {\em satisfying}.
nodes.statement_short: Decide whether positive $3$-literal clauses admit a truth assignment making each clause contain both a true and a false literal.

nodes.name: \NP-completeness of {\sc $3$-Colouring}
nodes.statement: It is well known that even {\sc $3$-Colouring} is \NP-complete~\cite{Lo73}.
conclusions: even {\sc $3$-Colouring} is \NP-complete

nodes.name: Gr\"otschel--Lov\'asz--Schrijver theorem for perfect graphs
nodes.statement: A classical result in the area is due to Gr\"otschel, Lov\'asz, and Schrijver~\cite{GLS84}, who showed that {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for perfect graphs.
conclusions: {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for perfect graphs

nodes.name: Strong Perfect Graph Theorem
nodes.statement: For example, the set~${\cal H}$ of minimal forbidden induced subgraphs for the class of perfect graphs consists of all odd holes and odd antiholes~\cite{CRST06}.
conclusions: the set~${\cal H}$ of minimal forbidden induced subgraphs for the class of perfect graphs consists of all odd holes and odd antiholes

nodes.name: Kr\'al', Kratochv\'{\i}l, Tuza and Woeginger dichotomy for $H$-free graphs
nodes.statement: Kr\'al', Kratochv\'{\i}l, Tuza, and Woeginger~\cite{KKTW01} classified the complexity of {\sc Colouring} for the case where~${\cal H}$ consists of a single graph~$H$. They proved that {\sc Colouring} on $H$-free graphs is polynomial-time solvable if~$H$ is an induced subgraph of~$P_4$ or $P_1+\nobreak P_3$ and \NP-complete otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Colouring on $H$-free graphs is polynomial-time solvable exactly when $H \ssi P_4$ or $H \ssi P_1+P_3$, and \NP-complete otherwise.
assumptions: the case where~${\cal H}$ consists of a single graph~$H$
conclusions: {\sc Colouring} on $H$-free graphs is polynomial-time solvable if~$H$ is an induced subgraph of~$P_4$ or $P_1+\nobreak P_3$ and \NP-complete otherwise

nodes.name: Blanch\'e et al. classification for $(H,\overline{H})$-free graphs
nodes.statement: To give another example, Blanch\'e et al.~\cite{BDJP16} determined the complexity of {\sc Colouring} for $(H,\overline{H})$-free graphs for every graph~$H$ except when $H=P_3+\nobreak sP_1$ for $s\geq 3$ or $H=P_4+\nobreak sP_1$ for $s\geq 2$.
assumptions: every graph~$H$ except when $H=P_3+\nobreak sP_1$ for $s\geq 3$ or $H=P_4+\nobreak sP_1$ for $s\geq 2$
conclusions: determined the complexity of {\sc Colouring} for $(H,\overline{H})$-free graphs

nodes.name: Golovach--Paulusma dichotomy for List Colouring on bigenic classes
nodes.statement: In contrast to the incomplete classifications for {\sc Colouring} and {\sc Precolouring Extension}, Golovach and Paulusma~\cite{GP14} showed a dichotomy for the complexity of {\sc List Colouring} on bigenic graph classes.
conclusions: a dichotomy for the complexity of {\sc List Colouring} on bigenic graph classes

nodes.name: Schindl's Theorem
nodes.statement: For $p\geq 1$, let $H_1,\ldots,H_p$ be graphs whose complement is not in~${\cal T}$. Then {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(H_1,\ldots,H_p)$-free graphs.
assumptions: let $H_1,\ldots,H_p$ be graphs whose complement is not in~${\cal T}$
conclusions: {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(H_1,\ldots,H_p)$-free graphs

nodes.name: Finiteness of the unknown connected pairs
nodes.statement: There are only finitely many pairs $(H_1,H_2)$ of connected graphs with $\{H_1,H_2\} \cap \{K_{1,3},P_5\}=\emptyset$, such that the complexity of {\sc Colouring} on $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs is unknown.
nodes.statement_short: Once neither forbidden graph is the claw or $P_5$, only finitely many connected pairs remain unclassified for Colouring.
conclusions: There are only finitely many pairs $(H_1,H_2)$ of connected graphs ... such that the complexity of {\sc Colouring} on $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs is unknown

nodes.name: Hardness for pairs with cycles or induced claws
nodes.statement: If~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ both contain at least one cycle~\cite{EHK98} or both contain an induced~$K_{1,3}$~\cite{Ho81}, then even {\sc $3$-Colouring} is \NP-complete.
assumptions: $H_1$ and~$H_2$ both contain at least one cycle
conclusions: even {\sc $3$-Colouring} is \NP-complete

nodes.name: Hardness for $(P_{22},C_3)$-, $(P_9,C_4)$- and $(2P_2,C_r)$-free graphs
nodes.statement: It is known that {\sc $4$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(P_{22},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{HJP14} and that {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(P_9,C_4)$-free graphs~\cite{GHP} and for $(2P_2,C_r)$-free graphs for all $r \geq 5$~\cite{KKTW01}.
nodes.origin_citation: Huang, Johnson & Paulusma 2015; Gaspers, Huang & Paulusma 2017; Král' et al. 2001
conclusions: {\sc $4$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(P_{22},C_3)$-free graphs
{\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(P_9,C_4)$-free graphs and for $(2P_2,C_r)$-free graphs for all $r \geq 5$

nodes.name: Hardness for $(4P_1,2P_1+P_2)$-free graphs
nodes.statement: {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(4P_1,2P_1+\nobreak P_2)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}
conclusions: {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(4P_1,2P_1+\nobreak P_2)$-free graphs

nodes.name: Hardness of {\sc $5$-Colouring} for $P_6$-free and $(P_6,K_6)$-free graphs
nodes.statement: It is known that {\sc $5$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $P_6$-free graphs~\cite{Hu16}. As~$K_6$ is not $5$-colourable, this means that {\sc $5$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(P_6,K_6)$-free graphs, as observed in~\cite{GJPS}.
conclusions: {\sc $5$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $P_6$-free graphs
{\sc $5$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(P_6,K_6)$-free graphs

nodes.name: Ramsey's Theorem
nodes.statement: Since~$H_2$ is $(K_6,4P_1)$-free, Ramsey's Theorem~\cite{Ra30} implies that~$|V(H_2)|$ is bounded by a constant.
nodes.statement_short: Ramsey's Theorem bounds the order of a graph with no large clique and no large independent set.
conclusions: $|V(H_2)|$ is bounded by a constant

nodes.name: Hardness of {\sc $3$-Colouring} for $(K_{1,5},C_3)$- and $(K_{1,3},C_r)$-free graphs
nodes.statement: It is known that {\sc $3$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(K_{1,5},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{MF96} and for $(K_{1,3},C_r)$-free graphs whenever $r \geq 4$~\cite{KKTW01}.
conclusions: {\sc $3$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(K_{1,5},C_3)$-free graphs and for $(K_{1,3},C_r)$-free graphs whenever $r \geq 4$

nodes.name: Hardness for $(K_{1,3},K_4)$-free graphs
nodes.statement: {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(K_{1,3},K_4)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}
conclusions: {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(K_{1,3},K_4)$-free graphs

nodes.name: \NP-completeness for $(2P_2,\overline{3P_2},\overline{T_{0,2,2}})$-free graphs
nodes.statement: {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(2P_2,\overline{3P_2},\overline{T_{0,2,2}})$-free graphs.
conclusions: {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(2P_2,\overline{3P_2},\overline{T_{0,2,2}})$-free graphs

nodes.name: \NP-completeness for $(2P_2,\overline{2C_3},\overline{C_3+P_4},\overline{2P_4},\overline{T_{0,0,4}})$-free graphs
nodes.statement: {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(2P_2,\overline{2C_3},\overline{C_3+P_4},\overline{2P_4},\overline{T_{0,0,4}})$-free graphs.
conclusions: {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(2P_2,\overline{2C_3},\overline{C_3+P_4},\overline{2P_4},\overline{T_{0,0,4}})$-free graphs

nodes.name: Characterization of hereditary classes by forbidden induced subgraphs
nodes.statement: It is readily seen that a graph class~${\cal G}$ is hereditary if and only if it there exists a set~${\cal H}$ such that every graph in~${\cal G}$ is ${\cal H}$-free. If the graphs of~${\cal H}$ are required to be minimal under taking induced subgraphs, then~${\cal H}$ is unique.
nodes.statement_short: Hereditary classes are exactly the ${\cal H}$-free classes, and the minimal forbidden set ${\cal H}$ is unique.
assumptions: If the graphs of~${\cal H}$ are required to be minimal under taking induced subgraphs
conclusions: ${\cal G}$ is hereditary if and only if it there exists a set~${\cal H}$ such that every graph in~${\cal G}$ is ${\cal H}$-free
${\cal H}$ is unique

nodes.name: Every connected graph other than the claw and $P_5$ is almost classified
nodes.statement: Every connected graph apart from~$K_{1,3}$ and~$P_5$ is almost classified.
assumptions: Every connected graph apart from~$K_{1,3}$ and~$P_5$
conclusions: Every connected graph apart from~$K_{1,3}$ and~$P_5$ is almost classified

nodes.statement: $({\cal C},X)$ has a satisfying truth assignment if and only if~$G_1$ has a colouring that respects~$L$ if and only if~$G_2$ has a colouring that respects~$L$.

conclusions: $({\cal C},X)$ has a satisfying truth assignment if and only if~$G_1$ has a colouring that respects~$L$ if and only if~$G_2$ has a colouring that respects~$L$

nodes.statement: $({\cal C},X)$ has a satisfying truth assignment if and only if~$G'_1$ has a $2n$-colouring if and only if~$G'_2$ has a $2n$-colouring.

conclusions: $({\cal C},X)$ has a satisfying truth assignment if and only if~$G'_1$ has a $2n$-colouring if and only if~$G'_2$ has a $2n$-colouring

nodes.statement: The graph~$G_1'$ is $(2P_2,\overline{3P_2},\overline{T_{0,2,2}})$-free.
conclusions: The graph~$G_1'$ is $(2P_2,\overline{3P_2},\overline{T_{0,2,2}})$-free

nodes.name: Proof of the finiteness theorem
nodes.statement:
We first make a useful observation. Let~$H$ be a tree that is not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$ or~$P_5$ and that is not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$. If~$H$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$4$ then it contains an induced~$K_{1,4}$. If~$H$ has maximum degree~$3$, then since~$H$ is connected and not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$, it must contain an induced~$S_{1,1,2}$. If~$H$ has maximum degree at most~$2$, then it is a path, and since it is not isomorphic to~$P_5$ and not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, it follows that~$H$ must be a path on at least six vertices. We conclude that if~$H$ is a tree that is not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$ or~$P_5$ and that is not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, then~$H$ contains~$K_{1,4}$ or~$S_{1,1,2}$ as an induced subgraph or~$H$ is a path on at least six vertices. Now let $(H_1,H_2)$ be a pair of connected graphs with $\{H_1,H_2\} \cap \{K_{1,3},P_5\}=\emptyset$. If~$H_1$ or~$H_2$ is an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, then {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs, as {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for $P_4$-free graphs (see, for example,~\cite{KKTW01}). Hence we may assume that this is not the case. If~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ both contain at least one cycle~\cite{EHK98} or both contain an induced~$K_{1,3}$~\cite{Ho81}, then even {\sc $3$-Colouring} is \NP-complete. Hence we may also assume that at least one of $H_1,H_2$ is a tree and that at least one of $H_1,H_2$ is a $K_{1,3}$-free graph. This leads, without loss of generality, to the following two cases. { f Case 1.} $H_1$ is a tree and $K_{1,3}$-free.\ Then~$H_1$ is a path. First suppose that~$H_1$ has at least~22 vertices. It is known that {\sc $4$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(P_{22},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{HJP14} and that {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(P_9,C_4)$-free graphs~\cite{GHP} and for $(2P_2,C_r)$-free graphs for all $r \geq 5$~\cite{KKTW01}. Hence we may assume that~$H_2$ is a tree. By the observation at the start of the proof, this implies that~$H_2$ contains an induced~$K_{1,4}$, $S_{1,1,2}$ or~$P_6$. Therefore~$H$ contains an induced~$4P_1$ or~$2P_1+
obreak P_2$. Since~$H_1$ is a path on at least~22 vertices, $H_1$ contains an induced~$4P_1$. As {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(4P_1,2P_1+
obreak P_2)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs. Now suppose that~$H_1$ has at most~21 vertices. By the observation at the start of the proof, $H_1$ is a path on at least six vertices. It is known that {\sc $5$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $P_6$-free graphs~\cite{Hu16}. As~$K_6$ is not $5$-colourable, this means that {\sc $5$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(P_6,K_6)$-free graphs, as observed in~\cite{GJPS}. Therefore we may assume that~$H_2$ is $K_6$-free. Recall that {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(2P_1+
obreak P_2,4P_1)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, which are contained in the class of $(P_6,4P_1)$-free graphs. Therefore we may assume that~$H_2$ is $4P_1$-free. Since~$H_2$ is $(K_6,4P_1)$-free, Ramsey's Theorem~\cite{Ra30} implies that~$|V(H_2)|$ is bounded by a constant. We conclude that both~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ have size bounded by a constant. { f Case 2.} $H_1$ is a tree and not $K_{1,3}$-free, and~$H_2$ is $K_{1,3}$-free and not a tree.\ Then~$H_1$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$3$ and~$H_2$ contains an induced cycle~$C_r$ for some $r\geq 3$. It is known that {\sc $3$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(K_{1,5},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{MF96} and for $(K_{1,3},C_r)$-free graphs whenever $r \geq 4$~\cite{KKTW01}. We may therefore assume that~$H_1$ is a tree of maximum degree at most~$4$ and that~$H_2$ contains at least one induced~$C_3$ but no induced cycles on more than three vertices. Recall that {\sc $4$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(P_{22},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{HJP14}. Hence we may assume that~$H_1$ is a $P_{22}$-free tree. As~$H_1$ has maximum degree at most~$4$, we find that~$H_1$ has a bounded number of vertices. By assumption, $H_1$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$3$. As {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(K_{1,3},K_4)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, we may assume that~$H_2$ is $K_4$-free. By the observation at the start of the proof, $H_1$ must contain an induced~$K_{1,4}$ or~$S_{1,1,2}$. Recall that {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for the class of $(2P_1+
obreak P_2,4P_1)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, which is contained in the class of~$(K_{1,4},S_{1,1,2},4P_1)$-free graphs. Hence we may assume that~$H_2$ is $4P_1$-free. Since~$H_2$ is $(K_4,4P_1)$-free, Ramsey's Theorem~\cite{Ra30} implies that~$|V(H_2)|$ is bounded by a constant. Again, we conclude that in this case both~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ have size bounded by a constant.
nodes.statement_short: Structural observation on trees, then exhaustive case analysis reducing to known \NP-hardness results and Ramsey's Theorem to bound $|V(H_1)|,|V(H_2)|$.

nodes.name: Structural observation on trees
nodes.statement: We first make a useful observation. Let~$H$ be a tree that is not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$ or~$P_5$ and that is not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$. If~$H$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$4$ then it contains an induced~$K_{1,4}$. If~$H$ has maximum degree~$3$, then since~$H$ is connected and not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$, it must contain an induced~$S_{1,1,2}$. If~$H$ has maximum degree at most~$2$, then it is a path, and since it is not isomorphic to~$P_5$ and not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, it follows that~$H$ must be a path on at least six vertices. We conclude that if~$H$ is a tree that is not isomorphic to~$K_{1,3}$ or~$P_5$ and that is not an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, then~$H$ contains~$K_{1,4}$ or~$S_{1,1,2}$ as an induced subgraph or~$H$ is a path on at least six vertices.
nodes.statement_short: Show every tree other than $K_{1,3}$ and $P_5$ and not $\ssi P_4$ contains $K_{1,4}$, $S_{1,1,2}$, or is a path on $\geq 6$ vertices.

nodes.name: Reduction to two cases
nodes.statement: Now let $(H_1,H_2)$ be a pair of connected graphs with $\{H_1,H_2\} \cap \{K_{1,3},P_5\}=\emptyset$. If~$H_1$ or~$H_2$ is an induced subgraph of~$P_4$, then {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs, as {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for $P_4$-free graphs (see, for example,~\cite{KKTW01}). Hence we may assume that this is not the case. If~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ both contain at least one cycle~\cite{EHK98} or both contain an induced~$K_{1,3}$~\cite{Ho81}, then even {\sc $3$-Colouring} is \NP-complete. Hence we may also assume that at least one of $H_1,H_2$ is a tree and that at least one of $H_1,H_2$ is a $K_{1,3}$-free graph. This leads, without loss of generality, to the following two cases.
nodes.statement_short: Discard $P_4$-subgraph and both-cyclic/both-clawed pairs, leaving two cases on which of $H_1,H_2$ is a tree.

nodes.name: Case 1 with $H_1$ a path on at least 22 vertices
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 1.} $H_1$ is a tree and $K_{1,3}$-free.\\ Then~$H_1$ is a path. First suppose that~$H_1$ has at least~22 vertices. It is known that {\sc $4$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(P_{22},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{HJP14} and that {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(P_9,C_4)$-free graphs~\cite{GHP} and for $(2P_2,C_r)$-free graphs for all $r \geq 5$~\cite{KKTW01}. Hence we may assume that~$H_2$ is a tree. By the observation at the start of the proof, this implies that~$H_2$ contains an induced~$K_{1,4}$, $S_{1,1,2}$ or~$P_6$. Therefore~$H$ contains an induced~$4P_1$ or~$2P_1+\nobreak P_2$. Since~$H_1$ is a path on at least~22 vertices, $H_1$ contains an induced~$4P_1$. As {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(4P_1,2P_1+\nobreak P_2)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(H_1,H_2)$-free graphs.
nodes.statement_short: For long paths $H_1$, invoke the $(P_{22},C_3)$/$(P_9,C_4)$/$(2P_2,C_r)$ and $(4P_1,2P_1+P_2)$ hardness results to get \NP-completeness.

nodes.name: Case 1 with $H_1$ a path on at most 21 vertices
nodes.statement: Now suppose that~$H_1$ has at most~21 vertices. By the observation at the start of the proof, $H_1$ is a path on at least six vertices. It is known that {\sc $5$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $P_6$-free graphs~\cite{Hu16}. As~$K_6$ is not $5$-colourable, this means that {\sc $5$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(P_6,K_6)$-free graphs, as observed in~\cite{GJPS}. Therefore we may assume that~$H_2$ is $K_6$-free. Recall that {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(2P_1+\nobreak P_2,4P_1)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, which are contained in the class of $(P_6,4P_1)$-free graphs. Therefore we may assume that~$H_2$ is $4P_1$-free. Since~$H_2$ is $(K_6,4P_1)$-free, Ramsey's Theorem~\cite{Ra30} implies that~$|V(H_2)|$ is bounded by a constant. We conclude that both~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ have size bounded by a constant.
nodes.statement_short: Force $H_2$ to be $(K_6,4P_1)$-free and apply Ramsey's Theorem to bound $|V(H_2)|$.

nodes.name: Case 2, bounding $H_1$
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 2.} $H_1$ is a tree and not $K_{1,3}$-free, and~$H_2$ is $K_{1,3}$-free and not a tree.\\ Then~$H_1$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$3$ and~$H_2$ contains an induced cycle~$C_r$ for some $r\geq 3$. It is known that {\sc $3$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(K_{1,5},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{MF96} and for $(K_{1,3},C_r)$-free graphs whenever $r \geq 4$~\cite{KKTW01}. We may therefore assume that~$H_1$ is a tree of maximum degree at most~$4$ and that~$H_2$ contains at least one induced~$C_3$ but no induced cycles on more than three vertices. Recall that {\sc $4$-Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(P_{22},C_3)$-free graphs~\cite{HJP14}. Hence we may assume that~$H_1$ is a $P_{22}$-free tree. As~$H_1$ has maximum degree at most~$4$, we find that~$H_1$ has a bounded number of vertices.
nodes.statement_short: Use $(K_{1,5},C_3)$, $(K_{1,3},C_r)$ and $(P_{22},C_3)$ hardness to make $H_1$ a $P_{22}$-free tree of bounded degree, hence of bounded order.

nodes.name: Case 2, bounding $H_2$ and concluding
nodes.statement: By assumption, $H_1$ contains a vertex of degree at least~$3$. As {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(K_{1,3},K_4)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, we may assume that~$H_2$ is $K_4$-free. By the observation at the start of the proof, $H_1$ must contain an induced~$K_{1,4}$ or~$S_{1,1,2}$. Recall that {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for the class of $(2P_1+\nobreak P_2,4P_1)$-free graphs~\cite{KKTW01}, which is contained in the class of~$(K_{1,4},S_{1,1,2},4P_1)$-free graphs. Hence we may assume that~$H_2$ is $4P_1$-free. Since~$H_2$ is $(K_4,4P_1)$-free, Ramsey's Theorem~\cite{Ra30} implies that~$|V(H_2)|$ is bounded by a constant. Again, we conclude that in this case both~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ have size bounded by a constant.
nodes.statement_short: Force $H_2$ to be $(K_4,4P_1)$-free and conclude via Ramsey's Theorem that both graphs have bounded order.

nodes.name: Proof of the $2n$-colouring equivalence
nodes.statement: Let $i\in \{1,2\}$. By Lemma~\ref{l-true}, we only need to show that~$G_i$ has a colouring that respects~$L$ if and only if~$G'_i$ has a $2n$-colouring. First suppose that~$G_i$ has a colouring~$c$ that respects~$L$. We extend~$c$ to a colouring~$c'$ of~$G'_i$ by setting $c'(k_\ell)=\ell$ for $\ell \in\{1,\ldots,2n\}$. Now suppose that~$G'_i$ has a $2n$-colouring~$c'$. As the $k$-type vertices form a clique, we may assume without loss of generality that $c'(k_\ell)=\ell$ for $\ell \in \{1,\ldots,2n\}$. Hence the restriction of~$c'$ to~$G_i$ yields a colouring~$c$ that respects~$L$.
nodes.statement_short: Both directions by extending/restricting the colouring across the $k$-type clique, on top of Lemma~\ref{l-true}.

nodes.name: Reduce to the list-colouring equivalence
nodes.statement: Let $i\in \{1,2\}$. By Lemma~\ref{l-true}, we only need to show that~$G_i$ has a colouring that respects~$L$ if and only if~$G'_i$ has a $2n$-colouring.
nodes.statement_short: Invoke Lemma~\ref{l-true} to reduce the claim to the equivalence between list colourings of $G_i$ and $2n$-colourings of $G'_i$.

nodes.name: Forward direction: extend a list colouring
nodes.statement: First suppose that~$G_i$ has a colouring~$c$ that respects~$L$. We extend~$c$ to a colouring~$c'$ of~$G'_i$ by setting $c'(k_\ell)=\ell$ for $\ell \in\{1,\ldots,2n\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend a list colouring of $G_i$ by colouring $k_\ell$ with colour $\ell$.

nodes.name: Reverse direction: restrict a $2n$-colouring
nodes.statement: Now suppose that~$G'_i$ has a $2n$-colouring~$c'$. As the $k$-type vertices form a clique, we may assume without loss of generality that $c'(k_\ell)=\ell$ for $\ell \in \{1,\ldots,2n\}$. Hence the restriction of~$c'$ to~$G_i$ yields a colouring~$c$ that respects~$L$.
nodes.statement_short: Normalize the colours on the $k$-type clique and restrict back to $G_i$ to obtain a list colouring.

nodes.name: Proof that $G_1'$ is $(2P_2,\overline{3P_2},\overline{T_{0,2,2}})$-free
nodes.statement: We will prove that~$\overline{G_1'}$ is $(C_4,3P_2,T_{0,2,2})$-free. Observe that in~$\overline{G_1'}$, the set of $x$-type vertices is a clique, the set of $C$-type vertices is a clique and the set of $k$-type vertices is an independent set. Furthermore, in~$\overline{G_1'}$, no $x$-type vertex is adjacent to a $C$-type vertex. {\bf $\mathbf{C_4}$-freeness.} For contradiction, suppose that~$\overline{G_1'}$ contains an induced subgraph~$H$ isomorphic to~$C_4$; say the vertices of~$H$ are $u_1,u_2,u_3,u_4$ in that order. As the union of the set of $x$-type and $C$-type vertices induces a $P_3$-free graph in~$\overline{G_1'}$, there must be at least two vertices of the~$C_4$ that are neither $x$-type nor~$C$-type. Since the $k$-type vertices form an independent set, we may assume without loss of generality that~$u_1$ and~$u_3$ are of $k$-type. It follows that~$u_2$ and~$u_4$ cannot be of $k$-type. As the set of $x$-type vertices and the set of $C$-type vertices each from a clique in~$\overline{G_1'}$, but~$u_2$ is non-adjacent to~$u_4$, we may assume without loss of generality that~$u_2$ is of $x$-type and~$u_4$ is of $C$-type. Then~$u_4$ is adjacent to the two $k$-type neighbours of an $x$-type vertex, which correspond to an even and odd colour. This is not possible as~$u_4$, being a $C$-type vertex, is adjacent in~$\overline{G_1'}$ to (exactly three) $k$-type vertices, which correspond either to even colours only or to odd colours only. We conclude that~$\overline{G_1'}$ is $C_4$-free. {\bf $\mathbf{3P_2}$-freeness.} For contradiction, suppose that~$\overline{G_1'}$ contains an induced subgraph~$H$ isomorphic to~$3P_2$. As the $C$-type vertices and $x$-type vertices each form a clique in~$\overline{G_1'}$, one edge of~$H$ must consist of two $k$-type vertices. This is not possible, as $k$-type vertices form an independent set in~$\overline{G_1'}$. We conclude that~$\overline{G_1'}$ is $3P_2$-free. {\bf $\mathbf{T_{0,2,2}}$-freeness.} For contradiction, suppose that~$\overline{G_1'}$ contains an induced subgraph~$H$ isomorphic to~$T_{0,2,2}$ with vertices $a_0,a_1,a_2,b_0,b_1,b_2,c_0$ and edges~$a_0b_0$, $b_0c_0$, $c_0a_0$, $a_0a_1$, $a_1a_2$, $b_0b_1$, $b_1b_2$. As the $k$-type vertices form an independent set in~$\overline{G_1'}$, at least one of $a_1,a_2$ and at least one of $b_1,b_2$ is of $x$-type or $C$-type. As the $x$-type vertices and the $C$-type vertices form cliques in~$\overline{G_1'}$, we may assume without loss of generality that at least one of $a_1,a_2$ is of $C$-type and at least one of $b_1,b_2$ is of $x$-type. As the $C$-type vertices and the $x$-type vertices each form a clique in~$\overline{G_1'}$, this means that~$c_0$ must be of $k$-type, $a_0$ cannot be of $x$-type and~$b_0$ cannot be of $C$-type. As $k$-type vertices form an independent set in~$\overline{G_1'}$, $a_0$ and~$b_0$ cannot be of $k$-type. Therefore~$a_0$ is of~$C$-type and~$b_0$ is of $x$-type. This is a contradiction, as $C$-type vertices are non-adjacent to $x$-type vertices. We conclude that~$\overline{G_1'}$ is $T_{0,2,2}$-free.
nodes.statement_short: Work in the complement $\overline{G_1'}$ and rule out $C_4$, $3P_2$ and $T_{0,2,2}$ separately by contradiction, using that $x$- and $C$-types are cliques and $k$-types independent.

nodes.name: Complement reformulation and type structure
nodes.statement: We will prove that~$\overline{G_1'}$ is $(C_4,3P_2,T_{0,2,2})$-free. Observe that in~$\overline{G_1'}$, the set of $x$-type vertices is a clique, the set of $C$-type vertices is a clique and the set of $k$-type vertices is an independent set. Furthermore, in~$\overline{G_1'}$, no $x$-type vertex is adjacent to a $C$-type vertex.
nodes.statement_short: Restate the goal in $\overline{G_1'}$ and record that $x$- and $C$-type vertices form cliques while $k$-type vertices are independent.

nodes.name: $C_4$-freeness of $\overline{G_1'}$
nodes.statement: {\bf $\mathbf{C_4}$-freeness.} For contradiction, suppose that~$\overline{G_1'}$ contains an induced subgraph~$H$ isomorphic to~$C_4$; say the vertices of~$H$ are $u_1,u_2,u_3,u_4$ in that order. As the union of the set of $x$-type and $C$-type vertices induces a $P_3$-free graph in~$\overline{G_1'}$, there must be at least two vertices of the~$C_4$ that are neither $x$-type nor~$C$-type. Since the $k$-type vertices form an independent set, we may assume without loss of generality that~$u_1$ and~$u_3$ are of $k$-type. It follows that~$u_2$ and~$u_4$ cannot be of $k$-type. As the set of $x$-type vertices and the set of $C$-type vertices each from a clique in~$\overline{G_1'}$, but~$u_2$ is non-adjacent to~$u_4$, we may assume without loss of generality that~$u_2$ is of $x$-type and~$u_4$ is of $C$-type. Then~$u_4$ is adjacent to the two $k$-type neighbours of an $x$-type vertex, which correspond to an even and odd colour. This is not possible as~$u_4$, being a $C$-type vertex, is adjacent in~$\overline{G_1'}$ to (exactly three) $k$-type vertices, which correspond either to even colours only or to odd colours only. We conclude that~$\overline{G_1'}$ is $C_4$-free.
nodes.statement_short: Assume an induced $C_4$; parity of the $k$-type neighbours of a $C$-type vertex gives a contradiction.

nodes.name: $3P_2$-freeness of $\overline{G_1'}$
nodes.statement: {\bf $\mathbf{3P_2}$-freeness.} For contradiction, suppose that~$\overline{G_1'}$ contains an induced subgraph~$H$ isomorphic to~$3P_2$. As the $C$-type vertices and $x$-type vertices each form a clique in~$\overline{G_1'}$, one edge of~$H$ must consist of two $k$-type vertices. This is not possible, as $k$-type vertices form an independent set in~$\overline{G_1'}$. We conclude that~$\overline{G_1'}$ is $3P_2$-free.
nodes.statement_short: An induced $3P_2$ would force an edge inside the independent set of $k$-type vertices.

nodes.name: $T_{0,2,2}$-freeness of $\overline{G_1'}$
nodes.statement: {\bf $\mathbf{T_{0,2,2}}$-freeness.} For contradiction, suppose that~$\overline{G_1'}$ contains an induced subgraph~$H$ isomorphic to~$T_{0,2,2}$ with vertices $a_0,a_1,a_2,b_0,b_1,b_2,c_0$ and edges~$a_0b_0$, $b_0c_0$, $c_0a_0$, $a_0a_1$, $a_1a_2$, $b_0b_1$, $b_1b_2$. As the $k$-type vertices form an independent set in~$\overline{G_1'}$, at least one of $a_1,a_2$ and at least one of $b_1,b_2$ is of $x$-type or $C$-type. As the $x$-type vertices and the $C$-type vertices form cliques in~$\overline{G_1'}$, we may assume without loss of generality that at least one of $a_1,a_2$ is of $C$-type and at least one of $b_1,b_2$ is of $x$-type. As the $C$-type vertices and the $x$-type vertices each form a clique in~$\overline{G_1'}$, this means that~$c_0$ must be of $k$-type, $a_0$ cannot be of $x$-type and~$b_0$ cannot be of $C$-type. As $k$-type vertices form an independent set in~$\overline{G_1'}$, $a_0$ and~$b_0$ cannot be of $k$-type. Therefore~$a_0$ is of~$C$-type and~$b_0$ is of $x$-type. This is a contradiction, as $C$-type vertices are non-adjacent to $x$-type vertices. We conclude that~$\overline{G_1'}$ is $T_{0,2,2}$-free.
nodes.statement_short: An induced $T_{0,2,2}$ forces adjacent $C$-type and $x$-type vertices, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Proof that $G_2'$ is $(2P_2,\overline{2C_3},\overline{C_3+P_4},\overline{2P_4},\overline{T_{0,0,4}})$-free
nodes.statement:
We will prove that~$\overline{G_2'}$ is $(C_4,2C_3,C_3+
obreak P_4,2P_4,T_{0,0,4})$-free. Observe that in~$\overline{G_2'}$, the set of $C$-type vertices is a clique, the set of $x$-type vertices is an independent set and the set of $k$-type vertices is an independent set. Furthermore, in~$\overline{G_2'}$, no $x$-type vertex is adjacent to a $C$-type vertex and every $x$-type vertex has degree~$2$. In fact, the union of the set of $x$-type vertices and the $k$-type vertices induces a disjoint union of $P_3$s in~$\overline{G_2'}$. { f $\mathbf{C_4}$-freeness.} For contradiction, suppose that~$\overline{G_2'}$ contains an induced subgraph~$H$ isomorphic to~$C_4$, say the vertices of~$H$ are $u_1,u_2,u_3,u_4$ in that order. As the union of the set of $x$-type and $C$-type vertices induces a $P_3$-free graph in~$\overline{G_2'}$, there must be at least two vertices of the~$C_4$ that are neither $x$-type nor~$C$-type. Since the $k$-type vertices form an independent set, we may assume without loss of generality that~$u_1$ and~$u_3$ are of $k$-type. It follows that~$u_2$ and~$u_4$ cannot be of $k$-type. As the set of vertices of~$C$-type form a clique in~$\overline{G_2'}$, at least one of $u_2,u_4$, say~$u_2$, is of $x$-type. If~$u_4$ is also of $x$-type, then~$u_2$ and~$u_4$ are $x$-type vertices with the same two colours in their list, namely those corresponding to~$u_1$ and~$u_3$. This is not possible. Thus~$u_4$ must be of $C$-type. Then~$u_4$ is adjacent to the two $k$-type neighbours of an $x$-type vertex, which correspond to an even and odd colour. This is not possible as~$u_4$, being a $C$-type vertex, is adjacent in~$\overline{G_2'}$ to (exactly three) $k$-type vertices, which correspond either to even colours only or to odd colours only. We conclude that~$\overline{G_2'}$ is $C_4$-free. { f $\mathbf{(2C_3,C_3+
obreak P_4,2P_4)}$-freeness.} For contradiction, suppose that~$\overline{G_2'}$ contains an induced subgraph~$H$ isomorphic to $2C_3$, $C_3+
obreak P_4$ or~$2P_4$. As the $k$-type and $x$-type vertices induce a disjoint union of~$P_3$s in~$\overline{G_2'}$, both components of~$H$ must contain a $C$-type vertex. This is not possible, as $C$-type vertices form a clique in~$\overline{G_2'}$. We conclude that~$\overline{G_2'}$ is $(2C_3,C_3+
obreak P_4,2P_4)$-free. { f $\mathbf{T_{0,0,4}}$-freeness.} For contradiction, suppose that~$\overline{G_2'}$ contains an induced subgraph~$H$ isomorphic to~$T_{0,0,4}$ with vertices $a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,c_0$ and edges $a_0b_0$, $b_0c_0$, $c_0a_0$, $a_0a_1$, $a_1a_2$, $a_2a_3$, $a_3a_4$. First suppose, that neither~$b_0$ nor~$c_0$ is of~$C$-type. Since the union of the set of $x$-type vertices and the $k$-type vertices induces a disjoint union of $P_3$s in~$\overline{G_2'}$ it follows that~$a_0$ is of $C$-type. Since~$b_0$ and~$c_0$ are not of $C$-type and no vertex of $C$-type has a neighbour of $x$-type in~$\overline{G_2'}$, it follows that~$b_0$ and~$c_0$ must be of $k$-type. This is not possible, because the $k$-type vertices form an independent set in~$\overline{G_2'}$. Now suppose that at least one of $b_0,c_0$ is of $C$-type. Since the vertices of $C$-type induce a clique in~$\overline{G_2'}$, it follows that no vertex in $A:=\{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4\}$ is of $C$-type. Since~$A$ induces a~$P_4$ in~$\overline{G_2'}$, but the union of the set of $x$-type vertices and the $k$-type vertices induces a disjoint union of $P_3$s in~$\overline{G_2'}$, this is a contradiction. We conclude that~$\overline{G_2'}$ is $T_{0,0,4}$-free.
nodes.statement_short: Work in $\overline{G_2'}$, where $x$- and $k$-type vertices induce a disjoint union of $P_3$s, and rule out each forbidden graph by contradiction.

nodes.name: Complement reformulation and type structure
nodes.statement: We will prove that~$\overline{G_2'}$ is $(C_4,2C_3,C_3+\nobreak P_4,2P_4,T_{0,0,4})$-free. Observe that in~$\overline{G_2'}$, the set of $C$-type vertices is a clique, the set of $x$-type vertices is an independent set and the set of $k$-type vertices is an independent set. Furthermore, in~$\overline{G_2'}$, no $x$-type vertex is adjacent to a $C$-type vertex and every $x$-type vertex has degree~$2$. In fact, the union of the set of $x$-type vertices and the $k$-type vertices induces a disjoint union of $P_3$s in~$\overline{G_2'}$.
nodes.statement_short: Restate the goal in $\overline{G_2'}$ and record that $x$- plus $k$-type vertices induce a disjoint union of $P_3$s.

nodes.name: $C_4$-freeness of $\overline{G_2'}$
nodes.statement: {\bf $\mathbf{C_4}$-freeness.} For contradiction, suppose that~$\overline{G_2'}$ contains an induced subgraph~$H$ isomorphic to~$C_4$, say the vertices of~$H$ are $u_1,u_2,u_3,u_4$ in that order. As the union of the set of $x$-type and $C$-type vertices induces a $P_3$-free graph in~$\overline{G_2'}$, there must be at least two vertices of the~$C_4$ that are neither $x$-type nor~$C$-type. Since the $k$-type vertices form an independent set, we may assume without loss of generality that~$u_1$ and~$u_3$ are of $k$-type. It follows that~$u_2$ and~$u_4$ cannot be of $k$-type. As the set of vertices of~$C$-type form a clique in~$\overline{G_2'}$, at least one of $u_2,u_4$, say~$u_2$, is of $x$-type. If~$u_4$ is also of $x$-type, then~$u_2$ and~$u_4$ are $x$-type vertices with the same two colours in their list, namely those corresponding to~$u_1$ and~$u_3$. This is not possible. Thus~$u_4$ must be of $C$-type. Then~$u_4$ is adjacent to the two $k$-type neighbours of an $x$-type vertex, which correspond to an even and odd colour. This is not possible as~$u_4$, being a $C$-type vertex, is adjacent in~$\overline{G_2'}$ to (exactly three) $k$-type vertices, which correspond either to even colours only or to odd colours only. We conclude that~$\overline{G_2'}$ is $C_4$-free.
nodes.statement_short: Rule out an induced $C_4$ using disjointness of the lists $L(x_i)$ and the parity of $C$-type neighbourhoods.

nodes.name: $(2C_3,C_3+P_4,2P_4)$-freeness of $\overline{G_2'}$
nodes.statement:
{ f $\mathbf{(2C_3,C_3+
obreak P_4,2P_4)}$-freeness.} For contradiction, suppose that~$\overline{G_2'}$ contains an induced subgraph~$H$ isomorphic to $2C_3$, $C_3+
obreak P_4$ or~$2P_4$. As the $k$-type and $x$-type vertices induce a disjoint union of~$P_3$s in~$\overline{G_2'}$, both components of~$H$ must contain a $C$-type vertex. This is not possible, as $C$-type vertices form a clique in~$\overline{G_2'}$. We conclude that~$\overline{G_2'}$ is $(2C_3,C_3+
obreak P_4,2P_4)$-free.
nodes.statement_short: Two components would each need a $C$-type vertex, contradicting that they form a clique.

nodes.name: $T_{0,0,4}$-freeness, case neither $b_0$ nor $c_0$ is $C$-type
nodes.statement: {\bf $\mathbf{T_{0,0,4}}$-freeness.} For contradiction, suppose that~$\overline{G_2'}$ contains an induced subgraph~$H$ isomorphic to~$T_{0,0,4}$ with vertices $a_0,a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,b_0,c_0$ and edges $a_0b_0$, $b_0c_0$, $c_0a_0$, $a_0a_1$, $a_1a_2$, $a_2a_3$, $a_3a_4$. First suppose, that neither~$b_0$ nor~$c_0$ is of~$C$-type. Since the union of the set of $x$-type vertices and the $k$-type vertices induces a disjoint union of $P_3$s in~$\overline{G_2'}$ it follows that~$a_0$ is of $C$-type. Since~$b_0$ and~$c_0$ are not of $C$-type and no vertex of $C$-type has a neighbour of $x$-type in~$\overline{G_2'}$, it follows that~$b_0$ and~$c_0$ must be of $k$-type. This is not possible, because the $k$-type vertices form an independent set in~$\overline{G_2'}$.
nodes.statement_short: If neither triangle-neighbour is $C$-type, both must be $k$-type, contradicting independence.

nodes.name: $T_{0,0,4}$-freeness, case some $b_0,c_0$ is $C$-type
nodes.statement: Now suppose that at least one of $b_0,c_0$ is of $C$-type. Since the vertices of $C$-type induce a clique in~$\overline{G_2'}$, it follows that no vertex in $A:=\{a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4\}$ is of $C$-type. Since~$A$ induces a~$P_4$ in~$\overline{G_2'}$, but the union of the set of $x$-type vertices and the $k$-type vertices induces a disjoint union of $P_3$s in~$\overline{G_2'}$, this is a contradiction. We conclude that~$\overline{G_2'}$ is $T_{0,0,4}$-free.
nodes.statement_short: Otherwise the path $a_1a_2a_3a_4$ would be an induced $P_4$ inside a disjoint union of $P_3$s.

nodes.name: Proof of the two main hardness theorems
nodes.statement: It is readily seen that {\sc Colouring} belongs to \NP. Then the first theorem follows from Lemma~\ref{l-truth} combined with Lemma~\ref{l-s1}, whereas the second one follows from Lemma~\ref{l-truth} combined with Lemma~\ref{l-s2}.
nodes.statement_short: Membership in \NP plus the reduction lemma combined with each forbidden-subgraph lemma.

nodes.name: Proof of the summary theorem
nodes.statement:
If~$\overline{H}$ contains a graph in $\{2C_3,C_3+
obreak P_4,3P_2,2P_4,T_{0,2,2},T_{0,0,4}\}$ as an induced subgraph, then {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(2P_2,H)$-free graphs due to Theorems~ef{t-1} and~ef{t-2}. We may therefore assume that~$\overline{H}$ is $(2C_3,C_3+
obreak P_4,3P_2,2P_4,T_{0,2,2},T_{0,0,4})$-free. (Note that $T_{1,1,3}+
obreak P_{2n-1}$ is $(2C_3,T_{0,2,2},T_{0,0,4})$-free.) Recall that~${\cal T}$ is the class of graphs every component of which is isomorphic to a graph~$T_{h,i,j}$ for some $1\leq h\leq i\leq j$ or a path~$P_r$ for some $r\geq 1$. Note that $\overline{2P_2}=C_4 
otin {\cal T}$. Therefore, if $\overline{H} 
otin {\cal T}$, then {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(2P_2,H)$-free graphs by Theorem~ef{t-schindl}. We may therefore assume that $\overline{H} \in {\cal T}$. Since~$\overline{H}$ is $2C_3$-free, $\overline{H}$ can contain at most one component that is not a path. Since~$\overline{H}$ is $(T_{0,2,2},T_{0,0,4})$-free, if~$\overline{H}$ does have a component that is not a path, then this component must be an induced subgraph of~$T_{1,1,3}$. The union of components of~$\overline{H}$ that are isomorphic to paths form an induced subgraph of~$P_{2n-1}$. Therefore~$\overline{H}$ is an induced subgraph of $T_{1,1,3}+
obreak P_{2n-1}$. It is known that {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for $(P_5,H)$-free graphs if~$\overline{H}$ is an induced subgraph of $2P_1+
obreak P_3$~\cite{Ma}, $P_1+
obreak P_4$ (this follows from the fact that $(P_5,\overline{P_1+P_4})$-free graphs have clique-width at most~$5$~\cite{BLM04}; see also~\cite{BBKRS05} for a linear-time algorithm), $P_2+
obreak P_3$~\cite{ML17}, $P_5$~\cite{HL}, $T_{0,0,1}+
obreak P_1$~\cite{KMP}, $T_{0,1,1}$~\cite{KMP}, $T_{0,0,2}$~\cite{KMP} or $sP_1+
obreak P_2$ for some integer $s\geq 0$~\cite{ML17}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorems~\ref{t-1} and~\ref{t-2}, then Schindl's Theorem plus component analysis inside ${\cal T}$ for part (i), and cite known polynomial cases for part (ii).

nodes.name: Discard complements containing the new hard subgraphs
nodes.statement:
If~$\overline{H}$ contains a graph in $\{2C_3,C_3+
obreak P_4,3P_2,2P_4,T_{0,2,2},T_{0,0,4}\}$ as an induced subgraph, then {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(2P_2,H)$-free graphs due to Theorems~ef{t-1} and~ef{t-2}. We may therefore assume that~$\overline{H}$ is $(2C_3,C_3+
obreak P_4,3P_2,2P_4,T_{0,2,2},T_{0,0,4})$-free. (Note that $T_{1,1,3}+
obreak P_{2n-1}$ is $(2C_3,T_{0,2,2},T_{0,0,4})$-free.)
nodes.statement_short: Use the two new hardness theorems to assume $\overline{H}$ avoids the six listed graphs.

nodes.name: Component analysis inside ${\cal T}$
nodes.statement:
Recall that~${\cal T}$ is the class of graphs every component of which is isomorphic to a graph~$T_{h,i,j}$ for some $1\leq h\leq i\leq j$ or a path~$P_r$ for some $r\geq 1$. Note that $\overline{2P_2}=C_4 
otin {\cal T}$. Therefore, if $\overline{H} 
otin {\cal T}$, then {\sc Colouring} is \NP-complete for $(2P_2,H)$-free graphs by Theorem~ef{t-schindl}. We may therefore assume that $\overline{H} \in {\cal T}$. Since~$\overline{H}$ is $2C_3$-free, $\overline{H}$ can contain at most one component that is not a path. Since~$\overline{H}$ is $(T_{0,2,2},T_{0,0,4})$-free, if~$\overline{H}$ does have a component that is not a path, then this component must be an induced subgraph of~$T_{1,1,3}$. The union of components of~$\overline{H}$ that are isomorphic to paths form an induced subgraph of~$P_{2n-1}$. Therefore~$\overline{H}$ is an induced subgraph of $T_{1,1,3}+
obreak P_{2n-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Schindl's Theorem, then show $\overline{H} \in {\cal T}$ forces $\overline{H} \ssi T_{1,1,3}+P_{2n-1}$.

nodes.name: Collect the known polynomial-time cases
nodes.statement:
It is known that {\sc Colouring} is polynomial-time solvable for $(P_5,H)$-free graphs if~$\overline{H}$ is an induced subgraph of $2P_1+
obreak P_3$~\cite{Ma}, $P_1+
obreak P_4$ (this follows from the fact that $(P_5,\overline{P_1+P_4})$-free graphs have clique-width at most~$5$~\cite{BLM04}; see also~\cite{BBKRS05} for a linear-time algorithm), $P_2+
obreak P_3$~\cite{ML17}, $P_5$~\cite{HL}, $T_{0,0,1}+
obreak P_1$~\cite{KMP}, $T_{0,1,1}$~\cite{KMP}, $T_{0,0,2}$~\cite{KMP} or $sP_1+
obreak P_2$ for some integer $s\geq 0$~\cite{ML17}.
nodes.statement_short: Cite the literature results establishing part (ii) of the theorem.

nodes.name: Construction of the List Colouring instance $(G_1,L)$
nodes.statement:
Let $(X,{\cal C})$ be an instance of {\sc Not-All-Equal $3$-Satisfiability} with positive literals only. We construct an instance $(G_1,L)$ of {\sc List Colouring} as follows. For each~$x_i$ we introduce a vertex, which we also denote by~$x_i$ and which we say is of {\em $x$-type}. We define $L(x_1)=\{1,2\}$, $L(x_2)=\{3,4\},\ldots,L(x_n)=\{2n-1,2n\}$. In this way, each~$x_i$ has one odd colour and one even colour in its list, and all lists~$L(x_i)$ are pairwise disjoint. For each~$C_j$ we introduce two vertices, which we denote by~$C_j$ and~$C_j'$ and which we say are of {\em $C$-type}. If $C_j=\{x_g,x_h,x_i\}$ with $L(x_g)=\{a,a+
obreak 1\}$, $L(x_h)=\{b,b+
obreak 1\}$ and $L(x_i)=\{c,c+
obreak 1\}$, then we set $L(C_j)=\{a,b,c\}$ and $L(C_j')=\{a+
obreak 1,b+
obreak 1,c+
obreak 1\}$. Hence each~$C_j$ has only odd colours in its list and each~$C_j'$ has only even colours in its list. To obtain the graph~$G_1$ we add an edge between every vertex of $x$-type and every vertex of $C$-type. Note that~$G_1$ is a complete bipartite graph with bipartition classes $\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$ and $\{C_1,\ldots,C_m\}\cup \{C_1',\ldots,C_m'\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduction turning a positive NAE-3SAT instance into a complete bipartite graph $G_1$ with a list assignment $L$ encoding variables by disjoint colour pairs.
input: Let $(X,{\cal C})$ be an instance of {\sc Not-All-Equal $3$-Satisfiability} with positive literals only.
output: $G_1$ is a complete bipartite graph with bipartition classes $\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$ and $\{C_1,\ldots,C_m\}\cup \{C_1',\ldots,C_m'\}$

nodes.name: Introduce $x$-type vertices with disjoint colour pairs
nodes.statement: For each~$x_i$ we introduce a vertex, which we also denote by~$x_i$ and which we say is of {\em $x$-type}. We define $L(x_1)=\{1,2\}$, $L(x_2)=\{3,4\},\ldots,L(x_n)=\{2n-1,2n\}$. In this way, each~$x_i$ has one odd colour and one even colour in its list, and all lists~$L(x_i)$ are pairwise disjoint.
nodes.statement_short: One vertex per variable, with list $\{2i-1,2i\}$ so lists are pairwise disjoint and mix parities.

nodes.name: Introduce $C$-type vertex pairs with parity-split lists
nodes.statement:
For each~$C_j$ we introduce two vertices, which we denote by~$C_j$ and~$C_j'$ and which we say are of {\em $C$-type}. If $C_j=\{x_g,x_h,x_i\}$ with $L(x_g)=\{a,a+
obreak 1\}$, $L(x_h)=\{b,b+
obreak 1\}$ and $L(x_i)=\{c,c+
obreak 1\}$, then we set $L(C_j)=\{a,b,c\}$ and $L(C_j')=\{a+
obreak 1,b+
obreak 1,c+
obreak 1\}$. Hence each~$C_j$ has only odd colours in its list and each~$C_j'$ has only even colours in its list.
nodes.statement_short: Two vertices per clause, one taking only odd and one only even colours of its three variables.

nodes.name: Join $x$-type to $C$-type completely
nodes.statement: To obtain the graph~$G_1$ we add an edge between every vertex of $x$-type and every vertex of $C$-type. Note that~$G_1$ is a complete bipartite graph with bipartition classes $\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}$ and $\{C_1,\ldots,C_m\}\cup \{C_1',\ldots,C_m'\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Add all $x$--$C$ edges, making $G_1$ complete bipartite.

nodes.name: Construction of the List Colouring instance $(G_2,L)$
nodes.statement: We also construct an instance $(G_2,L)$ where~$G_2$ is obtained from~$G_1$ by adding edges between every pair of vertices of $x$-type. Note that~$G_2$ is a complete split graph.
nodes.statement_short: Turn the $x$-side of $G_1$ into a clique, yielding a complete split graph $G_2$ with the same lists.

nodes.name: Extension of $G_1,G_2$ to $G'_1,G'_2$ by a $k$-type clique
nodes.statement: We now extend~$G_1$ and~$G_2$ into graphs~$G'_1$ and~$G'_2$, respectively, by adding a clique~$K$ consisting of~$2n$ new vertices $k_1,\ldots,k_{2n}$ and by adding an edge between a vertex~$k_\ell$ and a vertex~$u$ of the original graph if and only if $\ell\notin L(u)$. We say that the vertices $k_1,\ldots,k_{2n}$ are of {\em $k$-type}.
nodes.statement_short: Add a $2n$-clique whose vertex $k_\ell$ is joined to every $u$ with $\ell \notin L(u)$, converting list colouring into ordinary $2n$-colouring.
output: a clique~$K$ consisting of~$2n$ new vertices $k_1,\ldots,k_{2n}$

nodes.name: Remaining open pairs on at most four and five vertices
nodes.statement: For instance, if we forbid two graphs~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ with $|V(H_1)|\leq 4$ and $|V(H_2)|\leq 4$, then there are three open cases left, namely when $(H_1,H_2)\in \{(K_{1,3},4P_1),\allowbreak (K_{1,3},2P_1+\nobreak P_2),\allowbreak (C_4,4P_1)\}$ (see~\cite{LM15} and \figurename~\ref{fig:fourvertices}). If~$H_1$ and~$H_2$ are connected with $|V(H_1)|\leq 5$ and $|V(H_2)|\leq 5$, then there are four open cases left, namely when $H_1=P_5$ and $H_2\in \{\overline{C_3+2P_1},\overline{C_3+P_2},\overline{P_1+2P_2}\}$ (see~\cite{KMP} and \figurename~\ref{fig:fivevertices}) and when $H_1=K_{1,3}$ and $H_2=\overline{C_4+P_1}$ (see~\cite{ML17} and \figurename~\ref{fig:fivevertices}).
nodes.statement_short: Three open pairs remain on at most four vertices and four on at most five connected vertices.

nodes.name: Open cases for $(K_{1,3},H)$-free graphs
nodes.statement: The complexity of {\sc Colouring} for $(K_{1,3},H)$-free graphs is less clear. As mentioned in Section~\ref{s-intro}, the cases where $H\in \{4P_1,2P_1+\nobreak P_2,\overline{C_4+P_1}\}$ are still open. Moreover, $K_{1,3}$ is not almost classified, as the case $H=P_t$ is open for all $t\geq 6$ (polynomial-time solvability for $t=5$ was shown in~\cite{Ma13}).
nodes.statement_short: The claw is not almost classified: $H=P_t$ is open for every $t \geq 6$, besides three small open cases.

nodes.statement: Note that~$\overline{2C_3}$ is isomorphic to~$K_{3,3}$.

nodes.name: Consequences of Open Problem 1
nodes.statement:
Open Problem~ef{o-p5} shows the following.  egin{itemize} \item The open cases for {\sc Colouring} restricted to $(2P_2,H)$-free graphs and $(P_5,H)$-free graphs coincide.\[-10pt] \item The graph $H$ in each of the open cases is connected.\[-10pt] \item The number of minimal open cases is~$10$, namely when $\overline{H}\in \{C_3+

nodes.statement: As every graph~$H$ listed in Open Problem~\ref{o-p5} appears as an induced subgraph in both the graph~$G_1'$ and the graph~$G_2'$ defined in Section~\ref{s-hard}, we need new arguments to solve the open cases in Problem~\ref{o-p5}.
